\chapter{Answering, Meeting, Buying}
\label{ch:la-answering-meeting-buying}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I answer, I meet and I buy in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and read an English word by recovering the older sense of the Latin verb inside it.}

The chapter closes on emō: after learning it the reader produces all three first-person forms and all three third-person forms in sequence — respondeō, conveniō, emō and respondet, convenit, emit — recovers redeem and example from the root's older sense 'take', and ranks the four getting-verbs capiō, accipiō, obtineō, emō against dō, retrieving capiō and dō from chapters 39 and 37.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[respondeō, respondēre]{respondeō — to pledge back}

\label{lesson:LA-C43-respondeo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Exspectō} waited by looking out. This verb is what ends the waiting — and what a Roman heard in it was not \textquotedblleft{}reply\textquotedblright{} but something much more binding.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: respondeō — \textquotedblleft{}I answer\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Respondeō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I answer},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I reply.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{respondēre}, with a long \emph{ē} — \textbf{second conjugation}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{respondeō} — I answer
  \item \textbf{respondēs} — you answer, to one person
  \item \textbf{respondet} — he answers, she answers
  \item \textbf{respondēmus} — we answer
  \item \textbf{respondētis} — you answer, to several people
  \item \textbf{respondent} — they answer
\end{itemize}

The \emph{-eō} of the I-form and the long \emph{-ē-} everywhere after it are the mark of that class, exactly as in \textbf{obtineō}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Respondēre} is \emph{re-}, \textquotedblleft{}back,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{spondēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to pledge, to promise solemnly.\textquotedblright{} So an answer, at the root, is a \textbf{pledge given back} — you are not merely saying words, you are matching someone's undertaking with your own.

\emph{Spondēre} was a heavy word. Its relative in Greek is \emph{spond\'{\={e}}}, a \textbf{libation} — wine poured out to seal an agreement — and in the plural it simply means a truce. Promises were made by pouring.

The English family is unusually wide. Straight from this verb: \textbf{respond}, \textbf{response}, \textbf{responsible} (able to answer for a thing) and \textbf{correspond}, two people answering each other by letter. From \emph{spondēre} on its own: a \textbf{sponsor} is one who pledges. From its participle \emph{spōnsus} and \emph{spōnsa}, \textquotedblleft{}pledged,\textquotedblright{} English has \textbf{spouse} — a husband or wife is, etymologically, a promise. And \emph{dē-spondēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to promise \emph{away},\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{despondent}, the state of having given your hope to somebody else.

Set the verb among the ones you have. \textbf{Rogō} asks, \textbf{audiō} hears, \textbf{sciō} knows, \textbf{dīcō} says, and \textbf{respondeō} answers. Five verbs, one conversation — and \emph{audiō} is the one that made \textbf{obey}, through \emph{ob-audīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to listen toward.\textquotedblright{} Latin thought obeying was a kind of answering too.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}respondeō, respondēs, respondet\textquotedblright{} — I, you, he or she answers
  \item \textquotedblleft{}respondēmus, respondētis, respondent\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the conversation, in order — rogō, audiō, sciō, dīcō, respondeō
  \item what the root really means — to pledge
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I answer\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}they answer\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Respondeō}, \textbf{respondent}.) What are its two pieces, and what does the second one mean? (\emph{\textbf{Re-}} and \emph{\textbf{spondēre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to pledge.\textquotedblright{}) Why is a husband a \textbf{spouse}? (Because \emph{spōnsus} means \textbf{pledged}.) Which five verbs make the conversation? (\textbf{Rogō, audiō, sciō, dīcō, respondeō}.) And which verb means \textquotedblleft{}I wait\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Exspectō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[conveniō, occurrō]{conveniō and occurrō — coming together, running into}

\label{lesson:LA-C43-convenio}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Respondeō} answered by pledging back. This verb needs nothing new from you: both halves of it are already yours.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: conveniō — \textquotedblleft{}I meet\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Conveniō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I meet},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I come together with.\textquotedblright{} Fourth conjugation, because \textbf{veniō} is:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{conveniō} — I meet
  \item \textbf{convenīs} — you meet, to one person
  \item \textbf{convenit} — he meets, she meets
  \item \textbf{convenīmus} — we meet
  \item \textbf{convenītis} — you meet, to several people
  \item \textbf{conveniunt} — they meet
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: occurrō — \textquotedblleft{}I run into\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Occurrō} is the other kind of meeting: not arranged, but stumbled into. Third conjugation, like \textbf{currō}: \textbf{occurrō, occurris, occurrit, occurrimus, occurritis, occurrunt}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Convenīre} is \emph{con-}, \textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{venīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to come.\textquotedblright{} To meet is to \textbf{come together}. English has \textbf{convene}, \textbf{convention}, a \textbf{convent} (those who came together), and \textbf{convenient}, which began as things \emph{coming together} well. A \textbf{covenant} is this verb's present participle, picked up through Old French.

\emph{Occurrere} is \emph{ob-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward, against,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{currere}, \textquotedblleft{}to run.\textquotedblright{} To meet by chance is to \textbf{run into} — the English idiom says the same thing, and gives \textbf{occur}. A thought that \emph{occurs} to you has run at you.

That \emph{con-} is worth collecting. It sits on \textbf{cōgitō}, \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{} — \emph{con-} plus a verb of shaking, so thinking is shaking things together. It sits on \textbf{claudō}: \emph{conclūdere} shuts things in together, whence \textbf{conclude}. And it sits on \textbf{ferō}, where \emph{cōnferre} gives \textbf{confer} and \textbf{conference}, people carrying their views together — a compound inherits its parent's oddity, so \emph{cōnferre}'s past is \emph{contulī}, borrowing that second root exactly as \emph{ferō} does.

One more piece is already yours. Chapter 21 taught \textbf{volup est convēnisse}, \textquotedblleft{}it is a pleasure to have met.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Convēnisse} is this verb — you have been saying \emph{conveniō} for twenty-two chapters without knowing it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}conveniō, convenīs, convenit\textquotedblright{} — I, you, he or she meets
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}occurrō, occurris, occurrit\textquotedblright{} — I, you, he or she runs into
  \item \emph{Say it:} the verb inside each — veniō, currō
  \item \emph{Run through:} the meeting scene — \textquotedblleft{}Salvē! Quid agis?\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Valeō. Volup est convēnisse!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I meet\textquotedblright{}, arranged and by chance? (\textbf{Conveniō}, \textbf{occurrō}.) What are the pieces of each? (\emph{\textbf{Con}} plus \textbf{veniō}; \emph{\textbf{ob}} plus \textbf{currō}.) Which chapter-21 phrase holds this verb? (\emph{\textbf{Volup est convēnisse}}.) Which earlier verb is \emph{con-} plus a shaking-verb, and what does \emph{con-} plus \textbf{ferō} give English? (\textbf{Cōgitō}; \textbf{confer} and \textbf{conference}.) And which verb means \textquotedblleft{}I answer\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Respondeō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[emō, emere]{emō — buying, which used to be taking}

\label{lesson:LA-C43-emo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Conveniō} and \textbf{occurrō} wore their older verbs on the outside. This last one hides something instead, and its English children give it away.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: emō — \textquotedblleft{}I buy\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Emō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I buy}.\textquotedblright{} Short word, short vowels, third conjugation: \textbf{emere}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{emō} — I buy
  \item \textbf{emis} — you buy, to one person
  \item \textbf{emit} — he buys, she buys
  \item \textbf{emimus} — we buy
  \item \textbf{emitis} — you buy, to several people
  \item \textbf{emunt} — they buy
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}em-}}, and it did not mean \textquotedblleft{}buy.\textquotedblright{} It meant \textbf{take}. Buying is a late, narrow specialisation of taking — the same slide English makes when a shopper says \textquotedblleft{}I'll take it.\textquotedblright{}

The old sense never left the compounds, and that is where the payoff is. \textbf{Redimere} is \emph{red-} plus \emph{emere}, \textquotedblleft{}to take back\textquotedblright{} — to \textbf{buy back}. From it English has \textbf{redeem}, \textbf{redemption}, and, through French, \textbf{ransom}: literally a buying-back of a person. \textbf{Eximere} is \emph{ex-} plus \emph{emere}, \textquotedblleft{}to take out,\textquotedblright{} giving \textbf{exempt} — someone taken out of an obligation. Its noun \emph{exemplum} is \textquotedblleft{}a thing taken out\textquotedblright{} as a specimen, and English took that noun by two roads at once: as \textbf{example}, and, worn down through Anglo-French, as \textbf{sample}. \textbf{Praemium} is \emph{prae-} plus the same root, \textquotedblleft{}what is taken first,\textquotedblright{} and is English \textbf{premium}.

You have met this verb once before without being told. In the taking-verb lesson, \emph{sūmere} was taken apart as \emph{sub} plus \emph{emere}. That was this word.

Now set the three getting-verbs side by side, because Latin keeps them apart. \textbf{Capiō} takes. \textbf{Accipiō} receives what is handed over. \textbf{Obtineō} gets and holds. \textbf{Emō} takes by paying. And facing all four is \textbf{dō}, \textquotedblleft{}I give\textquotedblright{} — because a sale is both at once: one side gives, the other takes.

One flag, and it is the last in this book. English \textbf{buy} is Germanic, and unusually it has no secure relatives outside Germanic at all. The whole \emph{*h\textsubscript{1}em-} family reached English only as loans: redeem, ransom, example, premium.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}emō, emis, emit\textquotedblright{} — I buy, you buy, he or she buys
  \item this chapter's three \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms — respondeō, conveniō, emō
  \item the three \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms — respondet, convenit, emit
  \item the four ways of getting — capiō, accipiō, obtineō, emō
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give this chapter's three \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms, then the three \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Respondeō, conveniō, emō}; \textbf{respondet, convenit, emit}.) What did the root of \emph{emere} originally mean? (\textbf{To take}.) So what is a \textbf{redemption}, and what is an \textbf{example}? (A \textbf{buying back}; a thing \textbf{taken out}.) Which verb receives what is handed over, and which gets and holds? (\textbf{Accipiō}; \textbf{obtineō}.) And which verb faces them all by giving? (\textbf{Dō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
